items.title: Mistral has released Mistral Large 4, scoring 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; Fran...
items.content:
Mistral has released Mistral Large 4, scoring 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; France is back to having the most intelligent model from outside the US and China

@MistralAI has released Mistral Large 4 in Research Public Preview, with plans to release the weights of the 1T parameter (49B active) model at the end of October. It achieves 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, comparable to GPT-6 Luna (max, 38) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 39). It also achieves 50% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, level with GLM-5.3-Flash and ahead of models such as Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max).

Key benchmarking results for Mistral Large 4 Preview:

➤ Most intelligent model from outside the US and China: Mistral Large 4 Preview scores 38 on the Intelligence Index, comparable to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 39) and GPT-6 Luna (max, 38). This makes it the most intelligent model from outside the US and China, ahead of countries such as South Korea and the United Arab Emirates

➤ Level with GLM-5.3-Flash on cyber defense capability: Mistral Large 4 Preview scores 50 on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, level with GLM-5.3-Flash (50) and behind MiMo-V2.6-Pro (56). Once its weights are released, it will rank among the top three open weights models on the Cyber Index. Its strongest result is on CyberGym-E2E-AA, where it scores 82%, ahead of MiMo-V2.6-Pro (79%) and GPT-6 Luna (max, 78%)

➤ Over 4x the Cost per Task of similar-intelligence open weights models: Mistral Large 4 Preview costs $1.13 per Intelligence Index task with standard pricing of $1.36/$4.18 per 1M input/output tokens, with $0.14 per 1M cached input tokens. For the first two weeks, Mistral Large 4 Preview will be served at a 50% launch discount, bringing its Cost per Task down to $0.57. This is still more costly than GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.25) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, $0.27)

➤ Strong document and image reasoning: Mistral Large 4 Preview scores 19% on GDP.pdf, on par with MiMo-V2.6-Pro (19%) and behind Kimi K3 (22%). This is an 18-point improvement from Mistral Large 3, partly driven by improvements in their API, which now accepts 100 images per request, up from 8 for previous Mistral models

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 512k tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text and image input, with text output

➤ Pricing: $1.36/$4.18 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.14 per 1M cached input tokens), with 50% off for the first two weeks ($0.68/$2.09)

➤ Availability: Research Public Preview on Mistral's API, with open weights planned for the end of October

Talk to Claude the way you wo...
items.content:
I am surprised that people are surprised this is how I prompt Claude.

Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks -- give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out.

Back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, your prompt mattered a lot. Nowadays, it's much more important to communicate to the model:

1. What you want it to do
2. How much effort you want it to spend
3. How it should verify that it did the right thing

items.title: Ling 3.1 Flash makes large gains in intelligence over its predecessor, scoring 41 on the Artificial ...
items.content:
Ling 3.1 Flash makes large gains in intelligence over its predecessor, scoring 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with particular improvement in agentic capabilities

@AntLingAGI has released Ling 3.1 Flash, a reasoning model with 560B total parameters, 25B active parameters, and a 1M token context window. It scores 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, up from 20 from Ling 3.0 Flash, which launched in August. Ling 3.1 Flash is expected to be open weights, with Ant Group releasing the weights soon.

Key results:

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash improves agentic capabilities over its predecessor. With a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,622 and an AA-Briefcase Elo of 1,400, the model rivals peer models such as GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max). Ling 3.1 Flash also shows notable gains on AutomationBench-AA (62%) and Terminal-Bench v4.0 (33%).

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash scores +2 on AA-Omniscience, a 22 point improvements from Ling 3.0 Flash (-18). Compared to its predecessor, its accuracy rate rose from 18% to 29% while the hallucination rate fell from 44% to 38% at a similar attempt rate (56% to 58%), demonstrating the gain comes primarily from knowing more, not abstaining more. For comparison, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max) has a hallucination rate of 97%.

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash is a larger model than its predecessor, priced accordingly, but more token efficient. It has 560B total and 25B active parameters, up from 124B and 5.1B for Ling 3.0 Flash, and is priced at $0.30 / $0.90 per 1M input / output tokens, up from $0.075 / $0.22. It used 218M output tokens to run the Intelligence Index, 16% fewer than Ling 3.0 Flash (261M).

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash has a higher cost per task than some peers, but remains in the most attractive quadrant. Ling 3.1 Flash costs $0.99 per task, well above GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.42) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max, $0.32) but below Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) at $1.24.

Additional model details:

➤ Size: 560B total parameters, 25B active

➤ Context window: 1M tokens

➤ Pricing: $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $0.90 per 1M output tokens, with cached input at $0.06 per 1M (80% discount)

items.content_html:
Ling 3.1 Flash makes large gains in intelligence over its predecessor, scoring 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with particular improvement in agentic capabilities

@AntLingAGI has released Ling 3.1 Flash, a reasoning model with 560B total parameters, 25B active parameters, and a 1M token context window. It scores 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, up from 20 from Ling 3.0 Flash, which launched in August. Ling 3.1 Flash is expected to be open weights, with Ant Group releasing the weights soon.

Key results:

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash improves agentic capabilities over its predecessor. With a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,622 and an AA-Briefcase Elo of 1,400, the model rivals peer models such as GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max). Ling 3.1 Flash also shows notable gains on AutomationBench-AA (62%) and Terminal-Bench v4.0 (33%).

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash scores +2 on AA-Omniscience, a 22 point improvements from Ling 3.0 Flash (-18). Compared to its predecessor, its accuracy rate rose from 18% to 29% while the hallucination rate fell from 44% to 38% at a similar attempt rate (56% to 58%), demonstrating the gain comes primarily from knowing more, not abstaining more. For comparison, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max) has a hallucination rate of 97%.

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash is a larger model than its predecessor, priced accordingly, but more token efficient. It has 560B total and 25B active parameters, up from 124B and 5.1B for Ling 3.0 Flash, and is priced at $0.30 / $0.90 per 1M input / output tokens, up from $0.075 / $0.22. It used 218M output tokens to run the Intelligence Index, 16% fewer than Ling 3.0 Flash (261M).

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash has a higher cost per task than some peers, but remains in the most attractive quadrant. Ling 3.1 Flash costs $0.99 per task, well above GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.42) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max, $0.32) but below Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) at $1.24.

Additional model details:

➤ Size: 560B total parameters, 25B active

➤ Context window: 1M tokens

➤ Pricing: $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $0.90 per 1M output tokens, with cached input at $0.06 per 1M (80% discount)

➤ Availability: Accessible through Novita AI, with weights coming soon

"The scarce information of the time that was not public yet in 2019 was that scaling was working, and was working in a predictable way."

"He looked at GPT-2 and he said, 'We could add eight more zeros to this. Instead of thousands of dollars of compute, we could train this on millions or billions of dollars of compute, and maybe it would just keep improving steadily.'"

"That was the thing that he knew before anyone else by virtue of running the team that was working on scaling."

items.title: OpenAI Web Search debuts on the Artificial Analysis Search Index at 74, the 5th best provider behind...
items.content:
OpenAI Web Search debuts on the Artificial Analysis Search Index at 74, the 5th best provider behind Perplexity, Octen, Parallel and Brave

@OpenAI Web Search is the first integrated first-party search tool on our board. Instead of an agent calling a Search API in our Stirrup harness, GPT-5.6 Luna (medium reasoning) calls OpenAI's built-in web_search tool, and OpenAI runs the whole search loop inside one Responses API call. All setups use the same underlying model, GPT-5.6 Luna (medium reasoning).

At ~$0.05 per task, OpenAI Web Search costs less than Parallel (advanced, $0.06) and Perplexity (medium, $0.07), but about twice as much as Octen ($0.024), which scores 3 points higher.

Key benchmarking results for OpenAI Web Search (medium search context):

➤ 5th best provider on the Artificial Analysis Search Index: OpenAI Web Search scores 74, a 41-point lift over the same model with no search (33). It places 7th of 26 products, level with You . com (highlights), Nimble (standard) and Exa (auto) at 74, behind the three Perplexity variants (77 to 80), Octen (77), Parallel (advanced) and Brave (LLM context) at 75

➤ OpenAI Web Search performs best on AA-Omniscience, our proprietary factual answer benchmark, achieving 72% accuracy. This ranks 3rd of 26 search provider variants, within 1 point of the leader, Firecrawl (73%). BrowseComp, which needs multi-hop reasoning across several searches, is its weakest benchmark: at 73.5% it ranks 13th of 26, well behind the Perplexity variants and Octen (85% to 87%)

➤ OpenAI Web Search uses fewer tokens for the same tasks: OpenAI bills about 40k input tokens per task, search results included, against 125k for the leanest Search API on the board, Perplexity (low). Its model cost is among the lowest on the board, at about $0.009 per task

➤ Built-in search costs less per task than most Search APIs: At ~$0.05 per task, OpenAI Web Search is cheaper than 17 of the 25 Search API products on the board (median $0.067), including Parallel (advanced, $0.06) and Perplexity (medium, $0.07). Octen costs about half as much ($0.024) and scores 3 points higher

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium reasoning) with OpenAI's web_search tool and search_context_size set to medium, in one Responses API call

➤ Pricing: $10 per 1k web_search calls, plus the search content, which OpenAI bills as model input tokens

➤ Contamination: we block known contamination sources through the tool's domain filter

items.title: Forethought's @TomDavidsonX on the overlooked RSI scenario where AI never "fooms" but progress still...
items.content:
Forethought's @TomDavidsonX on the overlooked RSI scenario where AI never "fooms" but progress still accelerates 2–3x:

"When people say RSI, they're lazily assuming that it is gonna foom. Which is totally plausible."

"I distinguish the foom and the fizzle scenario. In the fizzle scenario you have that recursive loop, but because the ideas are getting so much harder to find, the RSI isn't too scary. To be honest, I still think it's pretty scary in that scenario. We're talking about 2X, 3X the pace of progress."

"Actually RSI is just scary, fizzle or foom."

"A lot of people at the frontier labs are really thinking it's the foom, so they're like, 'RSI, foom, it's all the same thing, and it's coming next year.'"
@forethought_org

items.title: Forethought’s @TomDavidsonX argues the real turning point for AI won’t be a researcher proving an ex...
items.content:
Forethought’s @TomDavidsonX argues the real turning point for AI won’t be a researcher proving an explosive feedback loop, it’ll be an incident the public can actually see:

"I'm skeptical that nerdy analyses about explosive feedback loops is gonna be what convinces the public. It's gonna be incidents. Hugging Face, government hacks."

"If it's just a nerd from Anthropic being like, 'We did the math, and we think this thing's gonna explode,' we've kind of already had them say that."

"The scariest possibility is, 'Let's make this a securitized government-led project, and no one's gonna know what we're using them for.' That's very, very dangerous concentration of power territory."

"To be clear, I wouldn't trust any government with this. The Democrats would be just as capable of coming up with reasons why they need to be the ones overseeing it."

"It was the AI safety community that was initially pushing against open source and against sharing things widely, which I think was a big mistake. That's one thing that OpenAI has always been really good on, 'Let's push it out,' which I think is great."
@forethought_org

items.content_html:
Forethought’s @TomDavidsonX argues the real turning point for AI won’t be a researcher proving an explosive feedback loop, it’ll be an incident the public can actually see:

"I'm skeptical that nerdy analyses about explosive feedback loops is gonna be what convinces the public. It's gonna be incidents. Hugging Face, government hacks."

"If it's just a nerd from Anthropic being like, 'We did the math, and we think this thing's gonna explode,' we've kind of already had them say that."

"The scariest possibility is, 'Let's make this a securitized government-led project, and no one's gonna know what we're using them for.' That's very, very dangerous concentration of power territory."

"To be clear, I wouldn't trust any government with this. The Democrats would be just as capable of coming up with reasons why they need to be the ones overseeing it."

"It was the AI safety community that was initially pushing against open source and against sharing things widely, which I think was a big mistake. That's one thing that OpenAI has always been really good on, 'Let's push it out,' which I think is great."

@forethought_org

items.title: .@kevinroose reveals 3 pivotal moments that changed the course of AI: Ilya's transformer eureka, Q*,...
items.content:
.@kevinroose reveals 3 pivotal moments that changed the course of AI: Ilya's transformer eureka, Q*, and Sam Altman’s firing:

"One of them has to be the moment where Ilya Sutskever shows up at the desk of this junior OpenAI researcher, Alec Radford, clutching a copy of Attention Is All You Need, and says, 'We have to experiment with this.'"

"Another moment is the evening in 2023 when a couple of researchers at OpenAI are sitting in a conference room looking at the reasoning traces from the first reasoning model, Q*, that displayed for the first time that you could tell an AI model to slow down and think step by step."

"Obviously, the moment of Sam Altman's firing and rehiring, the blip, is a big one. Had it not happened the way it did, things would look very different."

"Maybe Ilya Sutskever would still be at OpenAI. Maybe if they had carried out the coup and not brought Sam back, they would all have ended up working for Microsoft."

items.title: Forethought’s @TomDavidsonX explains how Anthropic could test whether a software-only singularity is...
items.content:
Forethought’s @TomDavidsonX explains how Anthropic could test whether a software-only singularity is coming by seeing how fast each new Claude can recreate its last year of AI progress:

"The first scary indicator is we're beginning to see an acceleration in internal algorithmic progress. That doesn't by itself tell you, is it gonna fully explode, or is it gonna be a brief acceleration."

"Literally going from Claude 5 to Claude 5.5 is something like a 2X in how efficient these experiments are running."

"In the limit, they could freeze all their internal code base from a year ago, and see how much AI can reproduce the whole set of improvements that they actually did. How does Claude 5 do that? How does Opus 5.5 do that? How does Opus 6 do that?"

"You get a trend in how efficiently AI could have re-sprinted their last year of progress. If you did experiments along those lines, you could build a case for, this is the returns curve, and that math just implies this thing can explode."
@forethought_org

items.title: We got Computer playing StarCraft against Computer, in real time. No pausing. The game keeps running...
items.content:
We got Computer playing StarCraft against Computer, in real time. No pausing. The game keeps running while each agent thinks.

Blue 2 – Red 5

Final match. Blue builds up safely, reaches 41 Dragoons, and moves out. Red is waiting with High Templar and hits the army with Psionic Storm. Blue hadn’t scouted what Red was building.

Computer assembled the whole setup: an OpenBW-based Brood War runtime on a VPS, a C++ bridge, and four gameplay tools per agent. Each agent receives its own fog-of-war-limited game state. Recording and camera control run separately; the agents aren’t given video input.

items.title: Forethought’s @TomDavidsonX says AI labs could almost mathematically calculate whether a software-on...
items.content:
Forethought’s @TomDavidsonX says AI labs could almost mathematically calculate whether a software-only singularity is coming, but they're the only ones with the data to know:

"The hardware loop is gonna be slow. Building fabs takes years. The scariest thing is that maybe even without the hardware loop, that's by itself enough to explode, and that is the thing which scarily is actually pretty plausible."

"The most important thing in the world right now is just the AI companies measuring their own internal data. They're the ones with the data. We can't know from the outside."

"How much effort did it take to double algorithmic efficiency in 2025? Did it require more effort to double in 2026? What happens if you throw in twice as much experimental compute? What happens if instead you throw in twice as much cognitive labor?"

"You could do experiments to map out the entire R&D production function for AI research. Almost mathematically calculate all the constants for how inputs of labor and compute turn into algorithmic progress."
@forethought_org

"It was this slow accumulation of things that made Dario and Daniela and their crew feel like they couldn't trust Sam, they couldn't trust Greg."

"I found evidence of him thinking about leaving OpenAI as far back as 2018 and 2019. So it was not like he rage quit and stormed out."

"He thought, 'This is the lab that's gonna make it to AGI, and does the world really need one more AGI lab?' Ultimately he just reached his breaking point. I think that was avoidable, but I don't think it would've been easy."

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google DeepMind's Séb Krier is more worried about the decay of institutions tha...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google DeepMind's Séb Krier is more worried about the decay of institutions than about AI killing everyone.

• AI risk discourse has become so totalizing that some people act like the power-seeking optimizers they fear
• Too much of the AI safety community is "a giant homogenous blob of correlated views," and anyone in SF with friends in that crowd is at least adjacent to it
• The Hugging Face incident comes down to the training regime, poor eval environments and bad engineering, not models trying to take over
• People who get rich and leave the labs often hit a crisis of meaning, looking for something to believe in or some equivalent of repentance
• Too many people treat AGI and ASI as a god, when machines can be smarter than humans without being literally magic

@theojaffee: "He lives in New York and not in San Francisco, so he's not going to the exact same parties with the exact same people and the exact same monoculture all the time."

@schisofrenia: "We have, like, literally just topic mode collapse in SF where we all talk about the same thing and largely the same takes about the same thing."

items.content:
Profound CEO @thejamescad says the next consumer every brand will fight to win won’t be human, it'll be the AI agent choosing on their behalf:

"This is by far the biggest platform shift in the history of marketing."

"Two years ago, myself and a co-founder had two core beliefs. The first is that agents will represent a very important new customer for every business on the planet. And the second, marketers won't just build for agents, they will build with agents."

"Today, we support a third of the Fortune 100, companies like Estée Lauder, companies like Comcast, companies like Ramp."

"I don't see a future where humans will manually browse the internet themselves in the same way that we have for the past 20 years. The agents will browse the web on our behalf and make selection decisions based on our preferences."

"Agents will be the next consumer that every brand on the planet cares about, and if you don't, you're gonna get left behind."
@profound

OpenAI Web Search costs ~$0.05 ...
items.content:
Total Cost per Task combines search cost and model inference cost. 

OpenAI Web Search costs ~$0.05 per task: ~$0.04 for search at $10 per 1k web_search calls and ~$0.009 for the model. Search makes up about 80% of the cost, close to the 74% median for Search APIs.

On Artificial Analysis Search Index vs. Cost per Task, OpenAI Web Search sits below the cost frontier. Octen reaches 77 at ~$0.024 per task, and Perplexity (medium) reaches 80 at ~$0.07.

Profound CEO @thejamescad says marketing to AI agents will require your own AI agents, like sending your Terminator to fight their Terminator:

"Marketing is the act of influence. Companies have been very effective at doing that for the last couple of hundred years when it's been focused on humans. But when you are trying to influence an agent, it's a totally different type of marketing."

"You might have looked at the photo of that steamer and said, 'Oh, it looks quite good.' But an agent is comparing it against 500 other products. All the details that you may have ignored, the agent will not ignore."

"The best way to create that marketing is with agents. It's like in Terminator where you have to get your own Terminator to go against the Terminators, but maybe less nefarious."
@profound

items.title: Profound CEO @thejamescad predicts marketers will need to create 10-100x more content by next year b...
items.content:
Profound CEO @thejamescad predicts marketers will need to create 10-100x more content by next year because AI agents consume 20-50 pages where humans might read 1 or 2:

"If you ask ChatGPT or Gemini to research that steamer, typically it will pull maybe an order of magnitude more information than a human typically would absorb."

"You might visit one or two webpages, whereas an agent would run through 20, 30, 50 different pages."

"There is this new insatiable demand from agents on the internet, and marketers have to satiate that demand by creating high quality, differentiated, extremely broad, yet specific marketing that is aimed at agents."

"The biggest misnomer is the acronym. You get this AEO, GEO label put on the category. I think that's such a red herring. The similarities stop with the rhyming of the acronyms. This becomes the entire marketing stack."

"If you want to stay relevant as a marketer, you'll need to create maybe 10x to 100x more marketing than you do today by this time next year."
@profound

The replies here are literally hundreds of people who got their reviews removed directly contradicting what Airbnb says here

I don't get why they don't just fix this? Everyone would love to see Airbnb have honest reviews and ratings you can trust

I think they're in some internal gridlock by MBAs who want to see revenue go up, not realizing that they're destroying a company

I hope they fix it!

items.title: LLMs frequently generate overused, repetitive phrases and stylistic clichés—often termed "slop"—that...
items.content:
LLMs frequently generate overused, repetitive phrases and stylistic clichés—often termed "slop"—that degrade text quality and make outputs immediately recognizable as artificial. Existing suppression techniques like a naive token banning causes severe collateral damage to unrelated vocabulary, while standard preference tuning often triggers diversity collapse and quality degradation.

This article develops and evaluates Antislop, an end-to-end framework designed to systematically detect and suppress repetitive patterns at both generation time and during model finetuning without compromising overall capabilities or vocabulary diversity.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/VZtNuxWnwI
items.author: @burkov
items.summary: Andriy Burkov summarizes the Antislop framework: an end-to-end approach to detecting and suppressing repetitive LLM output patterns (slop) at generation time and during finetuning, avoiding the collateral vocabulary damage of naive token banning and the diversity collapse of standard preference tuning.
items.reasoning: Technically substantive summary of a research contribution from a credible ML author, though engagement is modest and it shares existing work rather than original insight. Relevant to a recognized LLM output-quality problem.
items.summary_html: Andriy Burkov summarizes the Antislop framework: an end-to-end approach to detecting and suppressing repetitive LLM output patterns (slop) at generation time and during finetuning, avoiding the collateral vocabulary damage of naive token banning and the diversity collapse of standard preference tuning.
items.content_html:
LLMs frequently generate overused, repetitive phrases and stylistic clichés—often termed "slop"—that degrade text quality and make outputs immediately recognizable as artificial. Existing suppression techniques like a naive token banning causes severe collateral damage to unrelated vocabulary, while standard preference tuning often triggers diversity collapse and quality degradation.

This article develops and evaluates Antislop, an end-to-end framework designed to systematically detect and suppress repetitive patterns at both generation time and during model finetuning without compromising overall capabilities or vocabulary diversity.

items.title: There's a reason I've been porting so many classic games I liked to web with WASM and why this is ta...
items.content:
There's a reason I've been porting so many classic games I liked to web with WASM and why this is taking off now I think

Because it's way easier to just open a new tab, type the URL and start playing than...

Switching on a console or gaming PC, waiting for it to boot, installing the Xbox/PS/Windows/Steam updates, rebooting, finding the game in your library, then a game popup appears (new DLC!!!), click away popup, click [ PLAY ], game has to download the new 50GB updates for 30 minutes, wait, load game, takes ages, tap [ Online ], try find our friends in some convoluted way, [ Play ]

I think game and console developers do not realize people don't have time to do all this

Many of us are doing other stuff, then have a break, just want to jump into a game, play a bit with friends, and get out again! And decompiling games and porting them to WASM does exactly that!

items.title: TIL a crazy number of hotels is owned not by public stock holders, not by private owners, not even b...
items.content:
TIL a crazy number of hotels is owned not by public stock holders, not by private owners, not even by private equity funds, but by governments!

You don't see this easily, because you have to dig quite deep (or well dig upward actually) and they cover it up in lots of constructions

Like this hotel in Paris "Le Ballu", sounds French? Yes and it's owned by Hotels & Preference, which on paper is a French international hotel chain

Hotels & Preference itself is owned by the Louvre Hotels Group, sounds French too? Yes

But Louvre Hotels Group is owned by Jin Jiang International, that doesn't sound so French anymore? So it must be a Chinese company? Right?

No! It's the municipality of Shanghai!?

Yes the the local council of Shanghai somehow owns 539 hotels around the world including Raddison, Park Plaza, Vienna House, Golden Tulip, Campanile, Kyriad etc.

Other big government owners are the government of Dubai, Brunei and Qatar

So I added a filter [ Government-owned hotels ] and every hotel page shows the TRUE owner of a hotel, not just the chain!

Researchers have now found extremely high amounts of PFAS in the majority of Dutch tap water

It blows my mind that this is still considered a normal part of democracy.

If a single person or a small group of individuals did that, they would be prosecuted or, if they attacked a policeman, likely shot. But if a larger group does that, police don't do anything but just stand, look at them, and let them do all this barbarism.

As I said, it blows my mind that in 2026, these vandals and thugs are given carte blanche to do whatever they want with public property and public servants.
